Question: What is the most profound lesson you have learned from a challenging experience?
Answer: I learned this lesson while saving money for university. I have followed it ever since. It's a combination of “the longest journey, starts with the first step”, and “don't give up, you can do it” If you don't start, you will never finish. The task might seem insurmountable, but if you break it down into pieces, and just keep working, you will achieve your goals. When I was in grade 8, I had no money , and I needed to save for university tuition and room and board. I started mowing lawns, and shoveling snow, but it wasn't going to cut it. But once I had some money in the bank, I could see myself inching towards my goal. Then in grade 9, I got a job working 20 hours a week. The money came faster, but still not fast enough. I only had 3 years to save, and probably had only got 15% of what I needed, in grade 8 and 9. In the summer before grade 10 ,I worked 40 hours a week, and during grade 10, I worked 30 hours a week, that summer I worked 40 hours again. I could see everything moving up the yardstick, but I was still not going to make it. So for grades 11 and 12, I worked 40 hours a week, and 50 hours during the summer. I had enough money for the first year, but only a little for the next year . So I worked at cafeteria to save money for my next year. Then when the first year was over, I got a camp job, that paid room and board, and I worked 360–380 hours a month, with all that overtime , I not only had enough for the next year, but had saved enough for part of the year after. I set a goal, broke it into pieces, and watching the money grow gave me incentive. But it was tempting to spend it.

Question: Which country surprised you the most?
Answer: Kazakhstan, or rather the area around Almaty Kazakhstan. Because that is all I saw, and it's a huge country. I was there in 2011, it was an eye opening experience. The most eclectic city I have ever been to. I flew into a Muslim country, got picked up at the airport by a new coworker, taken to my apartment, to refresh after flying for more than 24 hours. Then they knocked on my door, and we walked to a nearby Italian restaurant to get something to eat. We had a nice bottle of Chianti with the pasta. The next morning walking down the street, to the office, I passed a Lamborghini dealership, then a corrugated steel shack, then a Gucci store, two more corrugated steel shacks, then an Armani store and a Mercedes dealership. There was a gorgeous brand new apartment building, and someone had built an extension onto their balcony, to double it's size, out of corrugated steel. At busy intersections, they had tunnels below the streets, these tunnels were lined with stores. One store was a combination toy and liquor store, something that I had never seen at home. That night we went to a Brazilian steakhouse, it was pretty much what I expected. I walked to the grocery store, pretty much like the ones at home, except that they sold alcohol. Surprisingly, in a muslim country, the pork was kept right next to beef. If I had problems with the language, I would phone a translator at the office, and tell them what I needed, and they would talk to them and explain what I wanted. Maybe 5 percent of the people I encountered spoke English. There are 3 official languages, Kazakh, Russian and English. You are required to keep your passport on you at all times, and one day I was walking with an expat, who had been in the country for 15 years. We were heading to an Irish pub, for St Patrick's Day. The police stopped us, and asked for our ID, he didn't have his passport. He phoned his wife, who is local, and she told the police what for. But they still wrote him up a ticket. They are rich because of oil and gas, but Almaty is in an earthquake zone, and they aren't allowed to build pipelines across known faults, so most of the city is heated with coal. First thing in the morning, your lungs seize up, and you can't see the end of the block. Its surrounded by high mountains, but you can't see them, except on clear days. Kazakhs are tall and the women wear stiletto heels. I'm 6′2″, I remember looking up to a woman on 4 inch heels in the elevator with me. The women dress far more stylish than I am used to, maybe the average woman dresses like this in New York, but they certainly don't in Las Vegas, LA, or Toronto. At the time, the style was skin tight, button up shirts, my translator had buttons pulled so tight that I was worried that I would lose an eye if the button popped. I asked her how she reconciled that with being Muslim. She said that the Koran tells you to dress modestly, and she was. This was typical office wear, along with miniskirts and high heels. She said if she wore something that stood out, like a bikini to the office, that would be immodest. After all, how could something everyone wore, be immodest. Almaty was home to the worlds tallest wooden church. Almaty means orchard, and they are the home of all of our apples. They had kinds you see nowhere else. It was a surprise.
